extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and appellants (patent litigators, patent prosecutors, and counsel handling PTAB appeals to the Federal Circuit)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on which issues from PTAB final written decisions may be appealed to the Federal Circuit and the applicable standards of review (de novo vs. substantial evidence), plus standing and interlocutory-appeal limitations. Useful for attorneys evaluating likelihood and strategy for appeals from IPR/CBMR/PGR proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to appeal the PTAB’s final written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: A “party dissatisfied with the final written decision” may appeal, but an appellant must have Article III standing—i.e., a concrete, particularized injury in fact—to invoke federal-court jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumer Watchdog v. Wi. Alumni Research Found.: statutory procedural rights (e.g., right to appeal) do not eliminate Article III requirements; a requestor’s denial of cancellation does not necessarily constitute injury in fact. The court left open whether preclusive/estoppel effects of a final PTAB decision could constitute injury in fact under different circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable standards of review under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, a reviewing court decides all relevant questions of law and must set aside agency actions, findings, and conclusions that are arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, not in accordance with law, or unsupported by substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). This framework establishes that legal questions and factual findings are treated differently on appeal from PTAB decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal conclusions reviewed de novo
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal conclusions reached by the PTAB are reviewed de novo by the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under de novo review the Federal Circuit gives no deference to PTAB legal conclusions. (E.g., In re Elsner, Merck & Co. v. Kessler.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual findings reviewed for substantial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual findings of the PTAB are reviewed under the substantial evidence standard: whether a reasonable mind might accept the evidence as adequate to support the finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial evidence review (e.g., In re Gartside; In re Adler). The Supreme Court in Dickerson v. Zurko held that agency fact-finding is reviewed under the APA (substantial evidence), not the clearer 'clearly erroneous' (court/court) standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency fact-finding deference (Dickerson v. Zurko principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the USPTO/PTAB is an administrative agency, its factual findings receive deference under the APA (substantial evidence) rather than the court/court 'clearly erroneous' standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dickerson v. Zurko explained the court/agency standard is less strict than court/court, mandating APA standards for USPTO review; differences are subtle but dispositive for deference to agency findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless error / prejudicial error rule
rubrics_metrics.description: On appeal, an appellant must show not only that error occurred but that the error was harmful (i.e., prejudicial and affected the decision below).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APA requires taking due account of the rule of prejudicial error (5 U.S.C. § 706); burden normally falls upon the party attacking the agency’s determination (In re Chapman; Shinseki v. Sanders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial/interlocutory PTAB decisions are generally not appealable
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the Federal Circuit are only appropriate from final written decisions on the merits; initial determinations (e.g., whether to institute proceedings) are generally non-appealable and mandamus is typically inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory bars: 35 U.S.C. § 314(d) and § 324(e) (institution decisions final and nonappealable). Cases: In re Dominion (non-institution not appealable), In re Procter & Gamble (no immediate review of institution), mandamus denials in MCM Portfolio, Telefonaktiebolaget, Redline Detection. Some interlocutory issues may be re-raised after a final written decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to institute an IPR trial (non-appealable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A challenger may not appeal the PTAB’s non-institution decision to the Federal Circuit; mandamus is not an appropriate vehicle to challenge non-institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Dominion Dealer Solutions: petitioner has no clear and indisputable right to challenge a non-institution decision directly in the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision instituting an IPR trial (lack of immediate jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction to hear requests for immediate review of the PTAB’s decision to institute or not to institute an inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Procter & Gamble Co.: mandamus is not proper to challenge institution of IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the one-year statutory bar in institution decisions (mandamus generally denied)
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges to institution based on the one-year statutory bar are not generally granted mandamus review; patent owners bear a heavy burden to obtain mandamus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re MCM Portfolio, LLC: mandamus denied; court explained heavy burden to establish appropriateness of mandamus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for additional discovery or supplemental evidence (interlocutory evidentiary rulings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mandamus petitions compelling the PTAB to grant additional discovery or accept supplemental evidence are rarely appropriate; such interlocutory evidentiary matters are typically for the PTAB and may be raised on appeal from a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Telefonaktiebolaget LM Ericsson (discovery) and In re Redline Detection (supplemental evidence): mandamus denied without prejudice to raising the issues after final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 — Patentable Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim is drawn to patent-eligible subject matter under § 101 is a question of law reviewed de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Ferguson, 558 F.3d 1359, 1363 (Fed. Cir. 2009): § 101 matters are legal questions for de novo review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 — Utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an application discloses a utility for a claimed invention is a question of fact reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Fisher, 421 F.3d 1365, 1369 (Fed. Cir. 2005): utility is a factual determination subject to substantial-evidence review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102 — Statutory-type double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting (statutory-type) is a question of law reviewed de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Fallaux, 564 F.3d 1313, 1316 (Fed. Cir. 2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102 — Anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation is a question of fact reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Morsa, 713 F.3d 104, 109 (Fed. Cir. 2013): anticipation = factual determination, substantial-evidence review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(b) — Public Use (and On-Sale Bar) — law with subsidiary facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether something is 'in public use' or 'on sale' under § 102(b) is a question of law with subsidiary issues of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Epstein, 32 F.3d 1559, 1564 (Fed. Cir. 1994): treated as legal questions that rely on underlying factual determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(b) — Experimental Use Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of the experimental use exception to § 102(b) issues is a question of law with underlying factual issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also discussed in In re Epstein; courts treat the ultimate legal question as dependent on subsidiary factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(f) — Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception and inventorship are questions of law that the court reviews de novo, though predicated on factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sewall v. Walters, 21 F.3d 411, 415 (Fed. Cir. 1994): conception/inventorship treated as legal issues for de novo review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(g) — Priority, Conception, Reduction to Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority of invention and its constituent issues (conception and reduction to practice) are questions of law predicated on subsidiary factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singh v. Brake, 317 F.3d 1334, 1340 (Fed. Cir. 2003).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 103 — Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claimed invention would have been obvious is a question of law based on factual determinations (scope/content of prior art, differences between prior art and claims, level of ordinary skill, objective indicia). The Board's compliance with legal standards is reviewed de novo and underlying factual determinations for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randall Mfg. v. Rea, 733 F.3d 1355, 1362 (Fed. Cir. 2013): mixed question—legal review de novo for legal standard, substantial-evidence review for facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 103 — Obviousness-type Double Patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness-type double patenting is a question of law reviewed de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Hubbell, 709 F.3d 1140, 1145 (Fed. Cir. 2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112 — Written Description
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claimed invention is supported by an adequate written description under § 112, ¶ 1, is a question of fact reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Owens, 710 F.3d 1362, 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112 — Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is a question of law based on underlying factual findings (i.e., mixed question).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Morsa, 713 F.3d 104, 109 (Fed. Cir. 2013): enablement reviewed as legal question grounded in facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112 — Indefiniteness (claim construction subset)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefiniteness, as a subset of claim construction, is a question of law reviewed without deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Packard, 2014 WL 1775996, *2 (Fed. Cir. May 6, 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112 ¶ 6 — Means-Plus-Function (whether claim is in MPF form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining whether a claim limitation is written in means-plus-function form is a question of law reviewed de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Aoyama, 656 F.3d 1293, 1296 (Fed. Cir. 2011).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112 ¶ 6 — Function and corresponding structure for MPF claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the claimed function and the corresponding structure for a means-plus-function limitation are matters of claim construction presenting issues of law reviewed de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Aoyama, 656 F.3d 1293, 1296 (Fed. Cir. 2011).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 120 — Effective filing date / entitlement to priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Entitlement to a parent's effective filing date under § 120 is a matter of law reviewed de novo, with the written description requirement (a factual question) reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Owens, 710 F.3d 1362, 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2013): § 120 is law with underlying factual issues (written description).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is a question of law reviewed de novo by the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Packard and related authority treat claim construction and its legal consequences (e.g., indefiniteness) as legal questions subject to de novo review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify issues being appealed to determine applicable standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A critical initial step in any appeal from a PTAB final written decision is to identify the procedural and substantive issues being appealed so the appropriate standard of review (and level of deference) can be ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once issues are identified, counsel can determine likelihood of success and which issues require showing harmful/prejudicial error on appeal.
